[BUYER MISTAKE TOPIC]: getting pre-qualified instead of pre-approved before house hunting
[WHY IT MATTERS]: pre-qualification isn't verified, so offers can fall through or lose to buyers with real pre-approval in competitive markets
[WHAT TO DO INSTEAD]: get a full pre-approval with verified income/credit/assets before making offers
[AGENT NAME]: Sofia Marchetti
[TONE]: direct/no-fluff
9.output:
HOOK
"Pre-qualified" is not the same as "pre-approved."

BODY
A lot of buyers start house hunting with a pre-qualification letter, thinking it's the same thing as an approval. It's not — pre-qualification is basically a guess based on what you told a lender, nothing's been verified yet. In a competitive market, sellers know the difference, and your offer can lose to a buyer who actually has a verified pre-approval.

FIX
Before you fall in love with a house, get a full pre-approval — verified income, credit, and assets, not just a conversation. It takes a little more time upfront, but it makes your offer actually competitive.

CLOSE
Follow for more things nobody tells first-time buyers before they start looking. Questions? Send me a DM. — Sofia

OBJECTION 1: "I don't want to pay a commission."
RESPONSE: "That's completely fair, and it's the main reason most people try FSBO. What I'd offer is a flat, transparent commission with full-service marketing behind it — so it's less about avoiding a cost and more about whether the exposure and paperwork protection are worth it for your specific situation."

OBJECTION 2: "I've already got some interest on my own."
RESPONSE: "That's great, genuinely — interest is the hard part. One thing worth mentioning: I also handle pre-vetting buyers, so only serious, qualified offers make it to you, which can save a lot of wasted time on lookers who were never going to close."

OBJECTION 3: "I don't need help, I can handle the paperwork myself."
RESPONSE: "A lot of people can, and I respect that. The paperwork itself isn't usually the hard part — it's the legal risk if something's missed. That's the piece I handle so nothing comes back to bite you after closing."

OBJECTION 4: "Agents are all the same, why would I pick you?"
RESPONSE: "Fair question. I'd rather show you than tell you — happy to walk you through exactly how I market a listing and what the flat commission actually covers, and you can decide for yourself if it's different from what you've seen before."

OBJECTION 5: "I'll just call you if I can't sell it myself."

"I want to walk you through the whole process up front so nothing feels like a surprise later.

STEP 1: PRE-APPROVAL
First, we get you pre-approved with a lender — that just means a bank looks at your finances and tells you exactly what you can borrow. It's free, it usually takes a day or two, and it's the first real step because it tells us your actual budget.

STEP 2: HOUSE HUNTING
Once we know your budget, we start touring homes that fit what you're looking for. This part can take anywhere from a few weeks to a few months — there's no rush, we go at your pace until something feels right.

STEP 3: MAKING AN OFFER
When you find the one, we write up an offer together — that's a formal proposal to the seller with your price and terms. I'll walk you through every part of it before it goes anywhere.

STEP 4: INSPECTION & APPRAISAL
Once an offer's accepted, two things happen: an inspection, where a professional checks the home for any issues, and an appraisal, where the lender confirms the home's actually worth what you're paying. Both protect you.

STEP 5: CLOSING
Finally, closing — that's just the day you sign the final paperwork and get your keys. It sounds intimidating, but by that point, everything's already been reviewed and agreed on.

Through every single one of these steps, I'm right here with you — you'll never be figuring anything out alone."

"Before we start touring homes, I want to make sure we get you set up with a lender — and I want to explain why that matters, not just tell you to go do it.

"Before we get into the numbers, I want to walk you through what a net sheet actually is — it's just an estimate of what you'd walk away with after all the costs of selling are subtracted from the sale price. It's not final, but it gives us a realistic picture to plan around.

AGENT COMMISSION
This is the fee paid to the agents involved in the sale — it's typically the largest line item, and it's something we'll have agreed on upfront, no surprises.

ESTIMATED CLOSING COSTS
These are various fees involved in finalizing the sale — things like title work and recording fees. They're fairly standard and we'll estimate them based on typical costs in our area.

REMAINING MORTGAGE PAYOFF
If there's still a balance on your mortgage, that gets paid off at closing directly from the sale proceeds — this is simply what's left owed to your lender.

TRANSFER TAXES
Some areas charge a tax when property ownership transfers — this varies by location, and I'll make sure we're using the correct local rate.

BUYER CONCESSIONS / CREDITS
Sometimes as part of negotiations, sellers agree to credit the buyer for certain costs or repairs — if that happens, it gets factored in here.

Just remember — this whole sheet is an estimate based on today's information. As we get closer to an actual offer, I'll update it with real numbers so you always know where things stand."

Seasonal slowdowns can mean more negotiating room with motivated sellers, and less competition from other buyers than you'd face in spring.
